Abstract:
# Introduction Modern web development pipelines are subject to high levels of cognitive friction because we face two antagonistic real-world operational limitations. To begin with, static application security testing (SAST) tools have reported false positive rates of over 70%. Furthermore, a commercial generative large language model (LLM) would generate input-syntactically-correct but input-semantically-incorrect or contract-breaking patches. These fundamental systemic problems call for a more effective solution.

# Solution In this paper, we propose Aegis One AI, an end-to-end, closed-loop Dev Sec Ops defense copilot that connect static analysis to autonomous repair using four coordinated pillars. It first employs an authorized Pre-Flight Scope Guard to establish deterministic perimeter boundaries. It then deploys a hybrid detection engine that leverage AST static taint propagation with dynamic fuzzing telemetry. It leverages a heterogeneous Security Knowledge Graph that links source code AST sinks, HTTP routes, and database entities to generate an explainable 6-factor composite risk priority. Lastly, it uses a containerized, 4-stage disposable Docker sandbox that establish contract-preserving validation with automatic state rollback upon regression. In addition, all security operations, patch synthesis, and validation decisions are cryptographically chained in a tamper-evident SHA-256 Merkle audit trail signed via Ed25519 digital keys.

# Evaluation Empirical evaluation conducted across a benchmark suite of 120 synthetic and enterprise web vulnerabilities found Aegis One AI achieves 94.6% precision, 92.8% recall (F1-score 93.7%), 91.5% semantic patch validity, and 98.4% regression-free automated deployment rate. The system should deliver far superior and more reliable than an ungrounded LLM repair and standalone static scanner.
Intro_P1: Modern web application topologies are rapidly evolving and now often include fast-pipeline CI/CD workloads. Evidence points to Agile turning up speed on the feature delivery side but also increasing the size of organizational attack surface. Static Application Security Testing (SAST) relies on fixed syntax-pattern heuristics that tend to blast overload with alert fatigue due to unfocused, high-volume backlogs where up to 75% of the alerts are in fact non-exploitable noise. Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST) can confirm exploitability on runtime but suffers from poor code coverage, ultimately leaving large microservice boundaries with no AST taint sink identification.
Intro_P2: The recent adoption of generative LLMs by developers is causing renewed interest in the APR problem. However, the use of unconstrained generative models to fix security critical vulnerabilities presents a host of secondary risks. Because foundation models are grounded in bulk data and do not have a models-of-models understanding of runtime dependency topology, generative fixes can generate regressions, forgot to generate required authorization checks, or create imagined software libraries. A security fix would probably need to be shown to be safe, backwards compatible, and contract-preserving before release.
Intro_P3: In response to these compelling vulnerabilities and threats, the research and implementation described in this paper aim to leverage Aegis One AI, an autonomous closed-loop defensive Dev Sec Ops architecture, to convert speculative generative recommendation into leverageable, mathematically prioritized, empirical software defense. Aegis One AI fuses static analysis, dynamic telemetry, graph-theoretic risk propagation, and containerized sandbox verification into a hermetically sealed cryptographic immutable log, as compared with a diff text snippet in a developer chat window.
Threat_Model: This analysis assumes an external attacker facing the public Internet as well as an authenticated malicious insider with application credentials that are low value and have minimal on-path value. The adversary will likely seek to use the most common web application attack vectors, such as Structured Query Language Injection, Cross-Site Scripting, Broken Object Level Authorization, or Server-Side Request Forgery. The analysis also considers the presence of an untrusted generative model, with stochastic output that may contain hallucinations, logic errors, or back doors. Prior to any dynamic probe or code mutation, Aegis One AI is validated against the security policy and authorization specification (AU) before the probe is allowed to access the system. Non-authorized probes are rejected with a 403 Forbidden response at the ingress gateway to avoid accidentally probing the production or 3rd-party cloud infrastructure.
Hybrid_Detection: Most traditional analyzers work in isolation, which can lead to high false-positive rates or code paths not examined at all. Aegis One AI puts these two approaches into a single integrated dual-engine pipeline. When the AST traversal leads to the path suspected of containing taint, Aegis One AI does not write a simple static finding. Instead, it pulls the relevant route handler params, URL arguments, and data types, transforming the static AST finding into a dynamic fuzzing hypothesis. The embedded OWASP ZAP API controller activates the dynamic fuzzing engine to validate the hypothesis formed from the AST traversal finding. To verify real code execution versus reflection, cryptographically valued canary strings are injected. If reflected into the HTTP response body without sanitation or if the response latency exceeds the delay threshold during injection, the dynamic harness is likely to confirm exploitability.
Knowledge_Graph: Isolated vulnerability scanners treat each vulnerability as an isolated incident and ignore the system topology of the vulnerable component. It is a fair bet that a SQL injection in a remote admin analytics page service that monitors audience metrics for an enterprise page website will present a significantly different enterprise risk profile than the same vulnerability in a payment processing microservice that stores personally identifiable information unencrypted. Aegis One AI exploits a heterogenous directed security knowledge graph (modeled in Neo4j and NetworkX) of dependencies between routes, functions, sinks, databases, and sensitive data objects, and leverages topological metrics integrated with observed vulnerability severity to generate a normalized composite priority metric, likely placing sinks available with verified dynamic exploitability and direct access to PII above hypothetical vulnerabilities in separate modules.
Patch_Synthesis: Starting with a high priority vulnerability, Aegis One AI will kick off Automated Program Repair. Rather than feeding raw source files into an unconstrained text model, the patch generation subsystem constrains top-level structure and semantics. Studies have found generative models often try to "bandaid" fixed-patch vulnerabilities by adding potentially insecure shortcuts (deleting unit tests, eliminating authentication middleware, turning off CSRF protections, etc.). Aegis One AI also applies a deterministic Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) filter to parse the created patch before serializing onto disk. If any refusal rule triggers, the patch is immediately rejected, and a constrained re-prompting cycle is likely to occur.
Sandbox_Validation: In order to keep sure that the generated patches will not endanger stability of the software, the Aegis One AI tool also needs to verify within a sandbox runtime container before the patch is applied to a system. Disposable Docker containers are created by frozen base images, with tight namespace isolation, resource quotas and capabilities removed. If any of these four verification steps fail, the rollback protocol will probably revert the workspace to the base, record the failure telemetry, and flag the failure mode to developer console.
Merkle_Audit: In enterprise setting, all automated the changes must have mathematical non-repudiation. The research show that the Aegis One AI has an append-only cryptographic log chain based on SHA-256. Furthermore, the implementation provides Ed25519 private key signature for verifying author non-repudiation across distributed CI/CD runners. Any re-writing of old log records will break the mathematical hash chain invariant, which will cause a security auditor to immediately claim.
Eval_Conclusion: For independent static scan, the recall is 82.1%, but it has been plagued by high false-positive rate, as it would recognize safe queries with string concatenation as potential threats. For independent dynamic scan, it has a high precision yet cannot explore unvisited routes and message consumers on the backend, and thus has a low recall of 58.4%. Combining AST taint analysis with dynamic canary fuzzing in Aegis One AI results in precision of 94.6% and recall of 92.8% with an F1-score of 93.7%. For code repair, we found that the ungrounded baseline introduces functional regressions to roughly half of the accepted repairs. While Aegis One AI achieves semantic patch validity of 91.5% and zero-regression deployment rate of 98.4% thanks to sandbox auto-rollback. Our work suggests that Aegis One AI highlights the need for automatically guided AI-assisted cybersecurity to push the research to go beyond ungrounded text generation.
